newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe not out yet - aides.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe not out yet - aides.

text.p: Despite rumours and increasing manoeuvring in his own camp, unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe has not written himself out as France's next premier if the centre-right wins the forthcoming general election, aides said on Wednesday.

The aides, acccompanying Juppe on a campaign swing to the northern city of Lille, told reporters the prime minister was not overly worried by speculation he would be forced to step down after the election, even if he led his camp to victory.
They said Juppe "had not ruled out succeeding himself" if his camp won the election with a respectable margin over its left-wing foes.

The latest published poll indicated the centre-right would get between 313 and 342 seats, the combined left 213-239 seats and the far-right National Front up to three seats in the June 1 run-off round of the vote for the National Assembly.

Juppe's aides said he was not impressed by a suggestion, fed by his own justice minister and sometimes political rival Jacques Toubon, that the next prime minister should be chosen from outside the ranks of professional politicians.
Toubon repeated his suggestion in Paris on Wednesday, saying: "I am not among those who believe there is an insurmountable wall between politicians and citizens."
There was no indication which possible candidates he had in mind.

The best known precedents for such an appointment in contemporary France were when the late President Charles de Gaulle picked his own bureau chief, Georges Pompidou, and later his foreign minister, Maurice Couve de Murville, to become prime ministers in the 1960s.
Neither had ever stood for elected office but both, especially Pompidou who later succeeded de Gaulle, had extensive political experience.
More conventional contenders for Juppe's job mentioned by the press in recent days include former Prime Minister Edouard Balladur and National Assembly president Philippe Seguin.
President Jacques Chirac, told the ruling coalition before flying off on an official visit to China on Wednesday that they should stop their internal squabbling.
It is because Juppe's fate has occupied centre-stage in the campaign for the May 25-June 1 election that Chirac warned ministers not to let polemics overshadow issues.

"Unfortunately, the serious debate worthy of our democracy...is often masked by polemics and soundbites, from both the coalition and the opposition, which end up being the only things the public remembers," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as telling the cabinet.
The most unpopular premier since 1958 because of budget austerity, record unemployment and an image as a cold technocrat, Juppe is under fire both from foes and some allies.
Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing repeated on television on Tuesday night that it would be dangerous to ignore the fact that the voters wanted to be "governed differently".

Confirming other surveys, a Sofres opinion poll for the weekly Le Pelerin showed that fellow Gaullist Seguin was the voters' favourite for the premiership should the right win, with Juppe trailing far behind.
